The story was broken by the New York Times. New York Times journalists Tripp Mickle and Ana Swanson got a tip from from "a tech industry contact"[1] in August. They worked sources and investigated until they were ready to break the story in October.Based on the photos that have been popping up, the tech industry contact could have been any one of the comparatively large number of people in position to observe what was going on.  [1]: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/podcasts/the-daily/nvidia-jensen-huang-affair-chinese-spy-trump.html?showTranscript=1reply

I don't think it's as simple as an intern that saw them holding hands and blurted it out. That's not how you get this level of detailed and nuanced information:
"That revelation came after The New York Times broke the story of how U.S. intelligence officers uncovered what they say was a plot by Alice Huang to use their relationship to funnel information to Beijing."There is almost certainly some level of coordination between said "intelligence officers" and these reporters to make this a public story. They are choosing to comment and provide details on this particular issue, and they are doing so strategically.reply

Of course it was not as simple as that. Investigative reporters earn their keep. They spoke to a lot of sources, including sources in US intelligence. But that is not unusual for any important story: people in government like to talk, even those who work in three-letter agencies, for a mix of personal and professional reasons.Your comment above implies that the answer to "Why now?" is: "Because covert powers so decided." There is nothing in the story that disproves that, but also nothing that requires it. The initial tip could have been ordered from above, but it could just as easily have come from any one of dozens if not hundreds of people, motivated by just about anything: grievance, envy, high-mindedness, malice, vanity.reply

For something like this, at this level, involving these geopolitical players, you can guarantee that anyone from a 3 letter agency talking to the New York Times is doing so with a specific goal in mind.reply

Look at leaks at Apple. Some people are holding onto hot information and want to blab. It doesn’t have to be some master plan.reply

comments: Woohoo, that's a release! My personal favorites:- Stabilize never type- Stabilize custom allocators- Introduced minimum publish age configurations, also known as dependency cooldowns. When the relevant config is set, the resolver ignores versions published more recently than that, unless they are already in Cargo.lock. (RFC 3923) docs #17335- cargo-install: now uses the existing lockfile in the .crate tarball by default. --locked in cargo install becomes a no-op. #17388reply

> cargo-install: now uses the existing lockfile in the .crate tarball by default. --locked in cargo install becomes a no-op. #17388Long time follower of this. Very grateful it's been implemented.reply

Dependency cooldowns receiving such a whiplash this year. Earlier everyone was advocating for them because of the supply chain attacks. Now, people are worried because you might miss 0 days if you use them.Nonetheless, the ability to set and configure it is a welcome feature.reply

You should do both: you should let normal updates cool down, and you should immediately patch security advisories.One of the biggest ergonomic problems with cooldowns is that many tools let the former goal obstruct the latter. Both should be part of the state machine of resolution itself, rather than things that get layered on.reply
You should use a cooldown. The effects of a supply chain attack are significantly worse than the effects of a 0 day. You can always make exceptions on a case-by-case basis.reply
Some of us were saying they didn't understand the endgame of everyone using cooldowns at the time. We mostly got told we were wrong though.reply

They seem to use some interesting techniques.ModelTokenMemoryUsage [Bytes] = Parameters * (BitsPerParameter/8)For a model with 145B parameters, this means:    Precision       GB       GiB
    2-bit         36.25     33.76
    3-bit         54.38     50.64
    4-bit         72.50     67.52
    6-bit        108.75    101.28
    8-bit        145.00    135.04
    16-bit       290.00    270.08
    32-bit       580.00    540.17


You have roughly a factor 8 in memory usage from 32 bit down to 4 bit precision. title: I'm making LLMs work on small and old devices (github.com/hyperionaidev)
comments: For the last five months or so, opus and fable have both been able to do this task as a soneshot prompt. An inference engine is almost pure compute and to a first approximation the only operation your hardware needs to support to do llm inference is multiplication [the rest of an inference engine is "some trig"].So to get any model working on $OLD_HARDWARE, the hardest part of the task is now sourcing the hardware itself and giving the agent ssh access -- a modern agent will be able to source a compiler, write the implementation, optimize it, test in qemu (or any other simulator) and push it onto the device.Example prompt: "write an inference engine for qwen3 0.6b in pure assembly that runs on this device. Write a script to attach the weights to the resulting binary. Prefix is supplied as a stream of u32 token IDs on stdin. The engine streams u32 token IDs on stdout."reply

I agree with you, and I'm using claude and other models heavily, the idea is not in the soneshot - because actually as you see in the logs I posted on github, it took around 107 + 50-ish experiments to figure out which models to run which and push the speed.I'm treating it as a search algorithm project, where I develop the methdology and search for pushing the limit of devices and searching in a big space of possible kernels and so for what works for a specific hardware.so I'm looking at it from a different prespective, it takes a lot of brute forcing, and claude can do this well, the whole game (to me) is which directions you push the model into to reduce the search space. and how that learning from very small and tight devices you can scale these techniques.But in essence, I don't disagree with your sentiment - the goal is not 0.6B models, these are extremely trivial as you mentioned and as I showed in the experiments, the goal is 16B+ models, and this as far as I've seen, requires smart methods to search for optimizations and customizations both to the model and inference engines.reply

first_paragraph: maxxing the ability to run different LLMs on the smallest devices possibleRun the biggest language model you can on the smallest hardware you own.TV boxes, old tablets, single-board computers and routers all have a CPU, some RAM and flash storage that sit idle most of the day. smolmaxxing finds the biggest model each of them can really run, then pushes it further with custom kernels, careful memory use and weights streamed from flash. Every number in this repo was measured on the device itself.Both devices run 8B and 16B mixture-of-experts models on about 1 GB of RAM by keeping only part of each model in memory and reading the rest from flash as it's needed.More devices (phones, single-board computers, routers) are coming. The techniques aren't tied to one box: the 1-bit kernel needs only basic NEON, and the flash streaming works on any Linux or Android device with more model than RAM.All of it is a patch on llama.cpp. The main ideas:docs/how-it-works.md has every technique with its me
